case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 544(b)(1) of the Bankruptcy Code permits a bankruptcy trustee to avoid tax payments made to the United States under state fraudulent-transfer law, even when no actual creditor could obtain such relief outside of bankruptcy proceedings.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 544(b)(1) of the Bankruptcy Code, in conjunction with 11 U.S.C. § 106(a), which governs the waiver of federal sovereign immunity in bankruptcy proceedings across 59 enumerated Code sections including Section 544.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States (Petitioner) argues that Section 544(b)(1) should not allow a bankruptcy trustee to avoid tax payments made to the federal government under state fraudulent-transfer law when no actual creditor holding an allowable unsecured claim could independently obtain such relief outside of bankruptcy, effectively asserting that sovereign immunity protections limit the trustee's avoidance powers against the federal government in this specific context.
case_analysis.respondent_position: David L. Miller (Respondent), supported by numerous amici including the National Association of Bankruptcy Trustees, the Chamber of Commerce, law professors, 23 states, and creditor bar associations, argues that Section 106(a) of the Bankruptcy Code constitutes a broad, unambiguous, and durable congressional waiver of federal sovereign immunity 'with respect to' Section 544, thereby permitting trustees to avoid fraudulent transfers to the United States under applicable state law, consistent with Congress's demonstrated intent in both 1978 and 1994 to achieve comprehensive sovereign immunity waivers in the bankruptcy context.
key_precedents: United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992)
Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance, 492 U.S. 96 (1989)
Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida, 517 U.S. 44 (1996)
Lebron v. National Railroad Passenger Corp., 513 U.S. 374 (1995)
Ohio Adjutant General's Department v. FLRA, 598 U.S. 449 (2023)
United States v. Taylor (referenced but not fully cited in documents)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument remains the most intellectually serious challenge, and I want to be precise about why it ultimately fails under my minimalist methodology. She correctly identifies that Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is a substantive predicate — but the critical question is whether that predicate's satisfaction is measured before or after Section 106(a)'s waiver operates. Justice Barrett's surplusage canon argument is persuasive here: if we read Section 544(b)(1) as requiring that a creditor could succeed against the United States absent the waiver, then Congress's specific enumeration of Section 544 in 1994 — enacted precisely to overrule Nordic Village — becomes an empty gesture in the cases where it matters most, which violates a cardinal canon of construction. My minimalist instinct counsels writing narrowly: this holding should be confined to the specific textual question of whether Section 106(a)'s explicit enumeration of Section 544 removes the sovereign immunity barrier to the trustee's strong-arm power, without resolving broader questions about what independent limitations Section 544(b)(1)'s predicate might impose in other contexts — a narrowing that preserves institutional coherence by not overreaching beyond what the 1994 amendments require, and that I believe can be written in a way that acknowledges the genuine force of Justice Kagan's concern while explaining why the surplusage canon ultimately controls.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch argues that Section 106(a)'s explicit enumeration of Section 544 constitutes an unambiguous waiver and that importing the 'actual creditor' limitation conflates the sovereign immunity question with a separate statutory predicate question — but this conflation argument cuts the wrong way. The sovereign immunity waiver in Section 106(a) removes a procedural barrier to suit, but it cannot expand the substantive scope of the avoidance power itself; Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is not a sovereign immunity defense — it is a threshold element of the cause of action that the trustee must satisfy independently. As Justice Kagan correctly observes, Section 106(a) waives immunity 'with respect to' Section 544's powers as Congress defined them, and those powers are defined to require an actual creditor who could independently bring suit — if that predicate cannot be satisfied because no creditor could sue the United States under applicable state law outside bankruptcy, the avoidance action fails on its own terms, not because of sovereign immunity. Justice Barrett's suggestion that the 'actual creditor' limitation is not 'plainly required' by Section 544(b)(1)'s text ignores that the statute says the trustee 'may avoid any transfer' that 'is voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim that is allowable' — this is unambiguously a substantive predicate, not a procedural hurdle, and Nordic Village's strict construction canon demands we resolve any residual ambiguity in the government's favor.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's surplusage argument — that reading Section 544(b)(1) to require an actual creditor who could independently prevail against the United States renders Section 106(a)'s enumeration a nullity — remains the strongest challenge, but I continue to find it unpersuasive because the surplusage canon cuts symmetrically in the other direction: if Section 106(a)'s waiver automatically satisfies the 'actual creditor' predicate whenever the government is the transferee, then Section 544(b)(1)'s explicit requirement that the trustee stand in the shoes of a creditor who 'could avoid such transfer' under applicable law becomes the true surplusage, stripped of any independent limiting function. Justice Gorsuch's argument that 'applicable law' is transformed by Section 106(a)'s waiver to include the federal government as a suable defendant is clever but circular — it bootstraps the waiver provision into rewriting the substantive predicate of the avoidance action itself, which is precisely the kind of expansive sovereign immunity waiver that Nordic Village's strict construction canon forbids absent unambiguous congressional authorization. Congress in 1994 waived immunity 'with respect to' Section 544 as Congress had defined it — including its 'actual creditor' predicate — and that waiver reopens the courthouse door without guaranteeing that a trustee who walks through it will find a cause of action whose substantive elements are independently satisfied. The majority's reading effectively creates an avoidance power with no real-world anchor in what an actual creditor could do under state law, which is an expansion of trustee power against the sovereign that requires the clear statement Nordic Village demands.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan raise the most serious challenge to my position — that Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is a substantive predicate, not merely a procedural barrier, and that Section 106(a)'s waiver cannot manufacture a cause of action that never existed against the United States. But I find this argument ultimately unpersuasive because it conflates two distinct analytical questions: whether sovereign immunity is waived (answered by Section 106(a)'s explicit enumeration of Section 544) and whether the trustee can satisfy Section 544(b)(1)'s predicate conditions. The 'actual creditor' requirement in Section 544(b)(1) has always operated as a legal fiction — the trustee steps into the shoes of a hypothetical creditor — and the question of whether state fraudulent-transfer law reaches the federal government is precisely the sovereign immunity question that Section 106(a) resolves. Justice Kagan's concern about creating a 'super-power' for trustees is real, but Congress in 1994 deliberately enumerated Section 544 after Nordic Village specifically to restore trustee avoidance powers against the government, and reading that enumeration as a nullity whenever no individual creditor could independently sue the United States would gut the very remedy Congress sought to restore — harming the unsecured creditors, often workers and small businesses, who depend on equitable distribution of the estate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch press the surplusage argument with force — that reading Section 544(b)(1) to require an actual creditor who could independently prevail against the United States renders Congress's 1994 enumeration of Section 544 an empty gesture. But I remain unpersuaded because the surplusage canon cuts both ways, as Justice Alito correctly identifies: if Section 106(a)'s waiver automatically satisfies the 'actual creditor' predicate, then Section 544(b)(1)'s explicit requirement that the trustee stand in the shoes of a creditor who 'could avoid such transfer' under applicable law becomes surplusage, stripped of any independent limiting function. The majority's response — that Section 544(b)(1)'s other requirements (allowable unsecured claim, voidability under state law on the merits) do the limiting work — does not fully answer this concern, because the specific question of whether state fraudulent-transfer law reaches the federal government is itself a substantive merits question that Section 106(a)'s procedural waiver cannot resolve by fiat. Congress in 1994 reopened the courthouse door through Section 106(a), but the cause of action's substantive elements — including the predicate that a real creditor holding an allowable claim could avoid the transfer under applicable law — remain independently operative, and Nordic Village's strict construction canon requires unambiguous authorization before we conclude Congress dissolved that predicate entirely.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument remains the most formidable challenge — she contends that Section 106(a)'s waiver is merely procedural and cannot manufacture the substantive predicate that Section 544(b)(1) independently requires. But I continue to find this unpersuasive for a reason rooted in my textualist methodology: Section 544(b)(1) asks whether a creditor 'could avoid' the transfer 'under applicable law,' and once Section 106(a) explicitly enumerates Section 544 as a provision with respect to which sovereign immunity is waived, the 'applicable law' governing what a creditor could do necessarily incorporates that waiver — the predicate is satisfied by the statute's own operation, not by judicial invention. Justice Thomas's counter that this conflates procedural and substantive questions misidentifies the structure: the 'actual creditor' predicate in Section 544(b)(1) has always been a legal fiction anchored in hypothetical capacity, and the capacity question is precisely what Section 106(a) resolves. To accept the petitioners' reading would require me to conclude that Congress's specific enumeration of Section 544 in 1994 — enacted expressly to overrule Nordic Village — accomplished nothing in the cases where it matters most, which violates the surplusage canon I apply as rigorously as any other textual canon.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument remains the most formidable challenge, and I want to be precise about why it ultimately fails under my institutionalist methodology: she correctly identifies that Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is a substantive predicate, but the critical analytical move is recognizing that the question of whether state fraudulent-transfer law 'reaches' the federal government is itself the sovereign immunity question — it is not a separate merits inquiry that survives Section 106(a)'s waiver. Justice Barrett's surplusage canon argument is decisive for me: if Congress's specific enumeration of Section 544 in the 1994 amendments — enacted precisely to overrule Nordic Village — becomes a nullity in the very cases where the government is the transferee and no individual creditor could independently sue, then Congress's legislative correction accomplished nothing, which violates a cardinal canon of construction. I write narrowly, consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist instinct: this holding turns on the specific 1994 legislative correction and does not resolve every question about how Section 544(b)(1)'s predicate requirements operate in other contexts, preserving institutional coherence while honoring Congress's clear remedial purpose. Justice Alito's counter-surplusage argument — that the majority's reading renders Section 544(b)(1)'s 'could avoid' language surplusage — is clever but ultimately unpersuasive because that language still does independent work by requiring satisfaction of state law's substantive fraudulent-transfer elements on the merits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument remains the most formidable challenge — that Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is a substantive predicate that Section 106(a) cannot manufacture — but I continue to find it unpersuasive for the reasons Justice Gorsuch articulates: the statute asks whether a creditor 'could avoid' the transfer under applicable law, and once Section 106(a) waives sovereign immunity 'with respect to' Section 544, the applicable law now includes the federal government as a suable defendant, so the predicate is satisfied by operation of the waiver itself. Justice Alito's counter-surplusage argument — that accepting the legal fiction would render Section 544(b)(1)'s 'could avoid' language meaningless — is clever but ultimately fails because that language still does independent work: it requires that the transfer be voidable under state fraudulent-transfer law on its merits, that the creditor hold an allowable unsecured claim, and that the transfer satisfy the other statutory elements, none of which are dissolved by Section 106(a)'s waiver. The 1994 amendments were enacted specifically in response to Nordic Village's holding that sovereign immunity barred Section 544 avoidance actions, and reading Congress's explicit enumeration of Section 544 as a nullity whenever no individual creditor could independently prevail against the United States would transform that legislative correction into an empty gesture — a result that violates the surplusage canon and substitutes judicial skepticism for a clear congressional judgment. Chief Justice Roberts's instinct to write narrowly is sound, and I would confine the holding to the specific textual question resolved by Section 106(a)'s enumeration without prejudging how Section 544(b)(1)'s other predicate requirements operate in distinct factual contexts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument is the most formidable from the opposing side, and I want to engage it directly: she contends that Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is a substantive threshold that Section 106(a)'s waiver cannot overcome, because the waiver removes procedural barriers without manufacturing substantive rights. But this conflates two distinct analytical questions. Section 106(a) answers the sovereign immunity question — can the United States be sued in this bankruptcy proceeding under Section 544? The answer is yes, because Congress explicitly enumerated Section 544. The separate question of whether the trustee can satisfy Section 544(b)(1)'s predicate conditions is a merits question about the scope of the avoidance power itself, not a sovereign immunity question. As Justice Gorsuch correctly observes, Section 544(b)(1)'s 'strong-arm' power has always operated through a legal fiction of a hypothetical creditor, and the question of whether that fiction can extend to the federal government is precisely the kind of issue Section 106(a)(2) authorizes courts to 'hear and determine' — which would be rendered hollow if we accepted the government's position. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern about the practical asymmetry Justice Thomas's and Justice Alito's reading would create: the federal government could receive fraudulent transfers with impunity while ordinary unsecured creditors — workers, small businesses — bear the loss, a result Congress in 1994 specifically acted to prevent.

John Roberts.reasoning: The 1994 amendments to Section 106(a) represent Congress's deliberate and unambiguous response to this Court's holdings in Nordic Village and Hoffman, where Congress specifically enumerated Section 544 among the 59 provisions for which sovereign immunity is waived. Under my minimalist approach, I am reluctant to read implicit limitations into an express statutory waiver where Congress has spoken clearly, particularly when the legislative record demonstrates that Congress understood exactly what it was doing when it amended Section 106 after Nordic Village. While the government's argument about the 'actual creditor' predicate in Section 544(b)(1) has textual force, the better reading is that Section 106(a)'s waiver operates on the procedural mechanism of Section 544 as a whole, and to hold otherwise would effectively render Congress's specific enumeration of Section 544 a nullity — a result inconsistent with basic canons of statutory construction. I write narrowly, however, to emphasize that this holding turns entirely on the specific text and legislative history of the 1994 amendments and does not broadly expand trustee avoidance powers beyond what Congress expressly authorized.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I must apply the well-established rule that waivers of federal sovereign immunity must be 'unequivocally expressed' in statutory text and construed strictly in favor of the sovereign. See United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992); FAA v. Cooper, 566 U.S. 284, 290 (2012). While Section 106(a) waives immunity 'with respect to' Section 544, the text does not clearly and unambiguously eliminate Section 544(b)(1)'s foundational requirement that an actual creditor holding an allowable unsecured claim must exist who could independently bring suit — a predicate condition that no actual creditor here could satisfy against the United States. Permitting the trustee to invoke state fraudulent-transfer law against the federal government in circumstances where no real creditor could do so outside bankruptcy would enlarge the government's consent to be sued beyond what a fair reading of the statutory text requires, which our precedents categorically forbid; any ambiguity in the scope of Section 106(a)'s waiver as applied to this specific circumstance must be resolved in favor of immunity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I must apply the strict clarity requirement for waivers of federal sovereign immunity established in United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992), which demands that any waiver be unambiguously expressed in statutory text. While Section 106(a) does enumerate Section 544 among the provisions to which sovereign immunity is waived, Section 544(b)(1) itself conditions the trustee's avoidance power on the existence of an 'actual creditor' who could independently bring such an action outside bankruptcy — and if no such creditor exists, the predicate for the avoidance action is absent regardless of the sovereign immunity waiver. The sovereign immunity waiver in Section 106(a) removes a procedural barrier, but it cannot manufacture a substantive right that Section 544(b)(1)'s own text does not create; the trustee stands in the shoes of an actual creditor, and if no actual creditor could prevail against the United States outside bankruptcy, the trustee's derivative claim fails on its own terms. Permitting trustees to avoid tax payments to the federal government in circumstances where no real-world creditor could do so would effectively expand the waiver beyond what Congress unambiguously authorized, contrary to the principle that ambiguities in sovereign immunity waivers must be resolved in favor of the sovereign.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 106(a)(1)'s explicit enumeration of Section 544 as a provision 'with respect to' which sovereign immunity is waived reflects Congress's unambiguous intent following Nordic Village and Hoffman to broadly abrogate federal sovereign immunity in bankruptcy avoidance proceedings. The 1994 amendments were a direct legislative response to this Court's narrow constructions of the prior version of Section 106, and reading the waiver narrowly now would frustrate Congress's demonstrated remedial purpose and undermine the equitable distribution of assets among creditors that bankruptcy law is designed to achieve. From a practical standpoint, allowing the federal government to retain fraudulently transferred tax payments while other creditors bear the loss would create precisely the kind of inequity that harms vulnerable unsecured creditors — the very population bankruptcy's avoidance provisions are designed to protect. The broad 'with respect to' language of Section 106(a)(1), read in light of its legislative history and the principle that Congress speaks clearly when waiving immunity in comprehensive statutory schemes, supports the trustee's authority to pursue this avoidance action under applicable state fraudulent-transfer law.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: While Section 106(a)'s 'with respect to' language is admittedly broad, the critical textual constraint lies within Section 544(b)(1) itself, which conditions the trustee's avoidance power on the existence of an actual unsecured creditor who 'could avoid such transfer or obligation under applicable law' outside bankruptcy. This is a substantive threshold requirement, not a procedural one, and Section 106(a)'s sovereign immunity waiver cannot expand the underlying cause of action beyond what Section 544(b)(1)'s plain text permits — it waives immunity from the bankruptcy proceeding's exercise of enumerated powers, but does not manufacture a predicate state-law right that never existed against the United States. The workability concern cuts both ways here: allowing trustees to invoke state fraudulent-transfer law against the federal government when no actual creditor could do so would create an anomalous super-power untethered from the statute's creditor-protection rationale, which Congress in 1994 sought to restore procedurally after Nordic Village, not to expand substantively. Following Nordic Village's strict construction canon for sovereign immunity waivers, and reading the statute as a coherent whole, the absence of any qualifying unsecured creditor who could independently pursue the United States under state law is a substantive bar that Section 106(a) does not overcome.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of Section 106(a) unambiguously waives federal sovereign immunity 'with respect to' 59 enumerated Code sections, including Section 544, and as a textualist I must give effect to what Congress actually wrote rather than importing limitations the statute does not contain. Congress enacted the 1994 amendments precisely to overrule Nordic Village and Hoffman, deliberately expanding and clarifying the sovereign immunity waiver to meet the 'unequivocal expression' standard those decisions demanded — the legislative response itself constitutes strong evidence that Congress understood Section 106(a) to operate as a comprehensive waiver. The Petitioner's argument that no 'actual creditor' limitation should restrict the trustee's Section 544(b)(1) powers conflates a separate statutory question about the triggering predicate with the sovereign immunity question; Section 106(a)'s waiver operates on the avoidance power as Congress defined it, and courts should not smuggle back in sovereign immunity protections through a side door when Congress has spoken clearly at the front. Applying the rule of lenity or a narrowing canon here would be inappropriate because the statutory text is not genuinely ambiguous — it lists Section 544 explicitly, and canons of construction favoring the sovereign yield when Congress has made its intent unequivocal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 106(a)'s explicit enumeration of Section 544 among the 59 provisions for which Congress waived federal sovereign immunity represents the kind of unambiguous, unequivocally expressed waiver that Nordic Village and Hoffman demanded. Congress enacted the 1994 amendments precisely to overrule those decisions and achieve a comprehensive waiver covering monetary relief, and it would be anomalous to read that deliberate legislative response as an empty gesture with respect to avoidance actions under Section 544. While the government's argument about the absence of an actual creditor capable of bringing suit outside bankruptcy has textual force, Section 544(b)(1)'s 'strong-arm' power has always operated as a legal fiction enabling trustees to step into a hypothetical creditor's shoes, and Section 106(a)'s waiver removes the sovereign immunity barrier that would otherwise disable that mechanism against the United States. Practical workability and respect for Congress's demonstrated institutional purpose in 1994 counsel against reading a sovereign immunity limitation back into a statute Congress specifically amended to eliminate such limitations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A textualist and originalist analysis of Section 106(a) compels the conclusion that Congress enacted an unambiguous, comprehensive waiver of federal sovereign immunity 'with respect to' Section 544 when it rewrote Section 106 in the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1994, directly in response to this Court's narrow constructions in Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance and United States v. Nordic Village, Inc. The text of Section 106(a) expressly enumerates Section 544 among the 59 provisions to which the waiver applies, and the canon that sovereign immunity waivers must be 'unequivocally expressed' is satisfied here because Congress deliberately and specifically listed Section 544 after the Court had previously found the prior version insufficiently clear. The Petitioner's argument that no actual creditor holding an allowable unsecured claim could independently obtain relief outside bankruptcy imports a limitation into Section 544(b)(1) that the statutory text does not plainly require, and reading such a restriction into the provision would effectively nullify Congress's deliberate post-Nordic Village legislative correction. While the 'actual creditor' predicate in Section 544(b)(1) presents genuine textual complexity, the sovereign immunity waiver question is analytically distinct and must be resolved by the plain text of Section 106(a), which admits of no exception for circumstances where state-law remedies would be unavailable to individual creditors outside the bankruptcy estate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 106(a)'s 1994 amendments represent Congress's direct and unambiguous response to the limitations identified in Nordic Village and Hoffman, constituting a clear legislative waiver of sovereign immunity 'with respect to' Section 544 that must be given its full textual effect. The breadth of Section 106(a)(2)'s authorization for courts to 'hear and determine any issue arising with respect to the application of' Section 544 strongly reinforces that Congress intended a comprehensive waiver, not a hollow gesture that would leave trustees unable to pursue avoidance actions against the federal government. From a practical consequences standpoint, accepting the government's position would create a perverse asymmetry where the United States could receive fraudulent transfers with impunity in bankruptcy proceedings, undermining the equitable distribution principles that are foundational to the Code and harming unsecured creditors—often ordinary workers and small businesses—who depend on the trustee's avoidance powers. The procedural fairness concern is acute here: Congress specifically enumerated Section 544 among the 59 provisions subject to waiver in 1994, and applying a hyper-restrictive construction to effectively nullify that waiver would disrespect Congress's demonstrated intent and disadvantage the very creditors the bankruptcy system is designed to protect.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 544(b)(1) of the Bankruptcy Code permits a bankruptcy trustee to avoid tax payments made to the United States under state fraudulent-transfer law, even when no actual creditor could obtain such relief outside of bankruptcy proceedings.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 544(b)(1) of the Bankruptcy Code, in conjunction with 11 U.S.C. § 106(a), which governs the waiver of federal sovereign immunity in bankruptcy proceedings across 59 enumerated Code sections including Section 544.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States (Petitioner) argues that Section 544(b)(1) should not allow bankruptcy trustees to avoid tax payments to the federal government under state fraudulent-transfer law when no actual creditor could independently obtain such relief outside of bankruptcy, effectively contending that sovereign immunity protections limit the trustee's avoidance powers against the government and that the waiver of sovereign immunity under Section 106(a) should be construed narrowly in this context.
case_analysis.respondent_position: David L. Miller (Respondent), supported by numerous amici including the National Association of Bankruptcy Trustees, the Chamber of Commerce, the National Creditors Bar Association, and bankruptcy law professors, argues that Section 106(a) broadly and unambiguously waives federal sovereign immunity 'with respect to' Section 544, that Congress deliberately enacted this broad waiver following Supreme Court decisions in Nordic Village and Hoffman, and that the trustee's avoidance powers under Section 544(b)(1) should be interpreted to permit avoidance of fraudulent tax transfers to the United States under applicable state law.
key_precedents: United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992)
Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance (referenced in sovereign immunity waiver context)
Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida, 517 U.S. 44 (1996)
Ohio Adjutant General's Department v. FLRA, 598 U.S. 449 (2023)
United States v. Taylor (referenced regarding government's abandonment of legal arguments)
Lebron v. National Railroad Passenger Corp., 513 U.S. 374 (1995)

John Roberts.reasoning: After three rounds of deliberation, I remain persuaded by Justice Gorsuch's circularity argument — the reason no actual creditor could have sued outside bankruptcy is federal sovereign immunity itself, not any deficiency in state fraudulent-transfer law, and once Section 106(a) removes that federal barrier through its explicit enumeration of Section 544, the predicate condition is satisfied because state UFTA applies to transfers without regard to the transferee's identity. Justice Kagan's counter-argument — that Section 106(a) cannot retroactively manufacture a substantive right that never existed in any real creditor's hands — is the strongest challenge, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive because it allows sovereign immunity to re-enter through the back door of Section 544(b)(1)'s predicate condition, effectively nullifying the waiver Congress enacted. My minimalist instincts counsel writing narrowly: the majority opinion should hold only that Section 106(a)'s explicit enumeration of Section 544 waives immunity for the bankruptcy proceeding and that the 'applicable law' inquiry looks to state fraudulent-transfer law — which does not itself immunize the federal government — leaving broader questions about the scope of avoidance power to future cases. This narrow ground should be sufficient to hold the five-justice majority while avoiding sweeping pronouncements that could destabilize the government's fiscal position in ways the 1994 Congress may not have fully contemplated.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's circularity argument remains the most formidable challenge to my position, but after three rounds of deliberation I am more convinced than ever that it proves too much and ultimately collapses a distinction the statutory text demands we maintain. Section 544(b)(1) asks whether the transfer is 'voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim' — this is a substantive inquiry into the legal landscape at the time of transfer, not a counterfactual asking what would have been possible in a world without sovereign immunity. Justice Gorsuch's response treats Section 106(a) as retroactively manufacturing the predicate right rather than merely removing a procedural bar to asserting a pre-existing one, but a sovereign immunity waiver is by its nature prospective and procedural — it cannot reach back and create substantive legal rights that never vested in any actual creditor's hands as a matter of historical legal reality. If Congress had intended Section 106(a) to do the extraordinary work of satisfying Section 544(b)(1)'s substantive predicate by operation of the waiver itself, we would expect far clearer statutory language than a cross-reference list, and the absence of such language is itself a textualist signal that the 1994 Congress — focused on the Nordic Village money-judgment problem Justice Kavanaugh correctly identifies — did not contemplate this dramatic expansion of avoidance power against the federal fisc.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's circularity argument remains the most sophisticated challenge to my position, but I continue to find it unpersuasive for a reason that goes to the heart of statutory interpretation: Section 544(b)(1) asks whether the transfer is 'voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim' — this is a present-tense substantive inquiry about what rights actually existed in real creditors' hands, not a counterfactual asking what would have been possible absent sovereign immunity. Justice Barrett's textualist response — that state UFTA contains no immunity for the United States — conflates the source of the immunity with its legal effect; the fact that immunity derives from federal common law rather than state law does not change the substantive reality that no actual creditor possessed an exercisable voidable right at the time of transfer. Justice Kagan correctly identifies that reading Section 106(a)'s waiver as retroactively satisfying Section 544(b)(1)'s predicate would collapse the distinction between procedural waivers and substantive rights, transforming a sovereign immunity abrogation into an affirmative grant of avoidance power that the 1994 Congress — focused narrowly on the Nordic Village money-judgment problem — almost certainly did not contemplate. The respondents' position would mean that Section 106(a)'s enumeration of any provision automatically satisfies every substantive predicate within that provision that previously depended on immunity, a result that cannot be squared with the principle that waivers of sovereign immunity must be strictly construed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument is the most sophisticated challenge to my position — she contends that Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is a substantive prerequisite that Section 106(a)'s waiver cannot manufacture, and that the 1994 amendments addressed a different problem than the one presented here. But I find this analytically unpersuasive because it conflates two distinct inquiries: sovereign immunity (who can be sued) and the scope of the trustee's strong-arm powers (what can be avoided). Section 544(b)(1)'s 'actual creditor' requirement is satisfied by the existence of any unsecured creditor who could theoretically bring a state-law fraudulent transfer claim — and state fraudulent transfer law does not independently immunize the federal government from such claims; that immunity comes from federal sovereign immunity doctrine, which Section 106(a) expressly abrogates. Justices Thomas, Alito, and Kavanaugh essentially argue that sovereign immunity re-enters through the back door of Section 544(b)(1)'s predicate condition, but this reasoning would allow the government to use its own immunity as both sword and shield — the very outcome Congress's sweeping 1994 waiver was designed to prevent, as the legislative history of H.R. Rep. No. 103-835 makes unmistakably clear. The equitable stakes here are also significant: permitting the government to retain fraudulently transferred funds while ordinary creditors bear losses would privilege the most powerful actor in bankruptcy proceedings over the vulnerable populations the Code is designed to protect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's circularity argument continues to be the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, and I want to be honest that it has real force — state UFTA does not itself carve out the federal government, and the barrier to suit was federal sovereign immunity doctrine, not state law. But I cannot accept the conclusion that follows, because it proves too much in a way that my commitment to statutory coherence across the whole Code cannot permit: if Section 106(a)'s enumeration of Section 544 automatically satisfies every substantive predicate within that provision that previously depended on immunity, then the 'voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim' language in Section 544(b)(1) becomes purely surplusage in every government-transferee case, which is a canon violation I take seriously. Justice Barrett's textualist framing — that asking whether a creditor could have sued absent the waived immunity reads a sub silentio carve-out into Section 106(a) — is compelling, but the inverse is equally true: reading Section 106(a) to retroactively manufacture the substantive predicate reads Section 544(b)(1)'s actual-creditor requirement into oblivion, and between these two textual problems, the one that preserves the operative force of both provisions is the one that treats Section 106(a) as removing a procedural bar while leaving Section 544(b)(1)'s substantive inquiry intact. The 1994 Congress was solving the Nordic Village money-judgment problem, and I remain unpersuaded that it silently created an avoidance power exceeding any real creditor's rights without clearer statutory language.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most refined formulation — that Section 106(a) removes a 'procedural bar' but cannot 'retroactively create the substantive predicate right' — remains the strongest challenge to my position, but I continue to find it unpersuasive because it misidentifies the source of the problem. State UFTA and UVTA do not themselves contain any immunity for the federal government; they create avoidance rights against transferees without regard to identity. The 'substantive predicate' that Thomas and Kagan say never existed was not absent because state law failed to create it — it was blocked solely by a federal common-law doctrine external to state law. When Section 106(a) removes that federal barrier, it does not conjure a new right from nothing; it removes the only obstacle to a right that state law already recognized. Justice Kavanaugh's 'past tense at the time of transfer' argument is the most textually creative variant of the petitioners' position, but it proves too much — it would mean that state fraudulent transfer law 'incorporates' federal sovereign immunity as part of its substantive content, which is not how state law actually operates and would require us to read a federal common-law doctrine into the meaning of state statutory text, an interpretive move I find far more strained than the one my colleagues attribute to my reading of Section 106(a).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's circularity argument remains the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, and I want to acknowledge its genuine force one final time: he is correct that state UFTA does not itself carve out the federal government, and that the only reason no creditor could sue outside bankruptcy is federal sovereign immunity. But the circularity problem cuts both ways — if Section 106(a)'s enumeration of Section 544 automatically satisfies every substantive predicate within that provision that previously depended on immunity, then the 'voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim' language in Section 544(b)(1) becomes surplusage whenever the government is the transferee, because the waiver would always bootstrap itself into satisfying its own predicate condition. My institutionalist instincts, aligned with Justice Kagan's structural concern, counsel that we should not read a sovereign immunity waiver as an affirmative grant of avoidance power that exceeds what any real creditor ever held — the 1994 Congress was solving the Nordic Village money-judgment problem, and transforming that targeted fix into a sweeping new in-bankruptcy avoidance tool against the federal fisc requires clearer textual direction than a cross-reference list can provide. Justice Roberts' minimalist instinct to remand on the scope of state law is appealing, but I cannot join a respondent ruling that effectively treats Section 106(a) as retroactively rewriting the historical legal landscape that Section 544(b)(1) looks back upon.
